intro: Philadelphia plays the first side of an orchestral Hungarian Rhapsody, recorded in 1936 and first released in July 1937. Commons attributes the arrangement to Karl Müller-Berghaus; the piano catalogue number does not make it the piano version.
question: What happens to the opening rhetoric when an orchestra replaces one piano?

cues.title: An arrangement on two sides
cues.text: The source identifies the Philadelphia Orchestra, Stokowski and Müller-Berghaus’s arrangement. This stream is part 1 only; it does not combine the two HMV sides.
cues.evidence: Commons gives the performers, arranger and Part 1; filename identifies HMV DB3086 / 2a03100.

cues.title: A sustained early crest
cues.text: The opening grows into a broad area of strong recorded weight. Compare sustained orchestral tone with Rachmaninoff’s separately struck piano gestures, allowing for the different recording media.
cues.evidence: Relative level stays high from 0:55 to 1:25, including −10.1 dB at 1:15. The source establishes orchestra versus piano; no individual instrumental assignment is inferred.

cues.title: The weight falls away
cues.text: This quieter continuation follows a substantial reduction in recorded level. Follow the phrase across the withdrawal instead of assuming that spaces between attacks have the same function as on a piano.
cues.evidence: The 1:30 boundary accompanies a fall from −10.9 dB at 1:25 to −24.5 at 1:30, remaining low through 1:40.

cues.title: A later renewed surge
cues.text: Later on the side, the sound gathers weight after a low stretch. The comparison map stops earlier: this passage is heard as part of the source side, not treated as the same moment in all versions.
cues.evidence: The 3:22 boundary lies between low windows at 3:10–3:15 and a rise to −14.8 dB at 3:25. The comparison is restricted to the common opening.

composer.background:
Liszt was born in Doborján, a German-speaking village in the Hungarian kingdom, where his father Adam worked on an Esterházy estate. Hungary remained his declared homeland, although German and French were his principal languages. Adam taught him piano before taking him to Vienna in 1822 for lessons with Carl Czerny, who had studied with Beethoven, and Antonio Salieri. The family moved to Paris the following year. The Conservatoire refused him admission as a foreigner; private teaching and public concerts supplied his education instead. His early career therefore joined two institutions that would remain distinct in his adult life: the disciplined lesson and the commercial concert platform.

Adam died in 1827, leaving the sixteen-year-old Liszt to support himself and his mother by teaching. Paris offered an education beyond the keyboard: Victor Hugo, the religious social thinker Félicité de Lamennais, Chopin and Berlioz belonged to his intellectual or musical circle. Hearing Paganini in 1832 suggested that a pianist might make technical difficulty carry the same theatrical force as the violinist’s leaps and harmonics. Liszt responded with prolonged practice and transcription: his piano version of Berlioz’s Symphonie fantastique, published in 1834, aimed to preserve orchestral detail.
composer.born: 22 October 1811, Doborján, Kingdom of Hungary (now Raiding, Austria)
composer.epithet: The touring pianist who made a single theme change character, and eventually stripped virtuosity down to a few unresolved notes.
